title: Why Transformers — The Problems with RNNs

questions.question: Why can't an RNN process a 1,024-token sequence in parallel on a GPU?
options: The tokenizer produces embeddings one at a time
GPUs cannot run more than a few hundred threads at once — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Each hidden state h_t depends on h_{t-1}, forcing 1,024 serial steps
RNN weight matrices are too large to fit in GPU memory
questions.explanation: An RNN computes h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t): step t cannot start before step t-1 finishes. That serial dependency chain is what wastes a GPU's parallel cores on long sequences, regardless of memory or embedding cost.

questions.question: What does the fixed-width hidden state in a classic encoder-decoder RNN force the model to do?
options: Squeeze the entire source sequence into one vector before the decoder sees anything
Store one hidden state per attention head
Discard tokens beyond a fixed context window
Recompute gradients for every layer at every step, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
questions.explanation: The encoder compresses a source sequence of any length down to a single fixed-size vector. A 5-token and a 500-token source end up in the same bottleneck shape, which is why long sequences lose information before the decoder ever runs.

questions.question: Self-attention removes the RNN's serial dependency. What does it cost in exchange?
options: Model accuracy on short sequences
The ability to train with backpropagation, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence
O(N^2) memory in the attention matrix as sequence length N grows
Compatibility with GPU hardware
questions.explanation: Recurrence was O(N) in time and memory. Attention trades that for O(1) serial depth (full parallelism) at the cost of an N x N attention matrix, which is O(N^2) in memory — the reason long-context transformers need tricks like sliding windows or Flash Attention.

questions.question: According to Chinchilla (2022), how does a transformer compare to an RNN of equal parameter count?
options: The RNN always wins because it needs less training data
They perform identically once both are fully trained
The transformer needs more data to train well, but always wins given enough tokens
Neither architecture benefits from additional training data past a point, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
questions.explanation: Transformers assume no locality bias — every pair of tokens is a candidate for attention — so they need more data than an RNN to learn useful patterns. But given enough tokens, Chinchilla found a transformer always outperforms an RNN of the same size.

questions.question: Vanishing gradients made long-range dependencies unreliable in RNNs. What specifically causes this?
options: The attention matrix grows quadratically with sequence length — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Information from 50 tokens back is compressed through 50 non-linearities before it reaches the current step
LSTMs and GRUs cannot be trained with backpropagation
The tokenizer merges distant tokens into a single embedding
questions.explanation: Each recurrent step pushes the hidden state through another non-linearity. Fifty steps back means fifty compressions, and gradients (and the original signal) shrink at each one — gated units like LSTM/GRU soften this but don't eliminate it.

questions.question: What is the best completion criterion for Why Transformers — The Problems with RNNs?
options: Implement the core component without relying on a transformer framework
Skip validation and trust the first plausible-looking output
Choose a production framework before defining the core mechanism, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Treat one successful example as proof that every edge case works
questions.explanation: “Implement the core component without relying on a transformer framework” is one of this lesson’s stated outcomes; the other choices bypass its required reasoning or validation.
